item.title: Week 5 - Social influences and deductive models
item.description:
In this week, we got to consider social factors in habitation choices of people in the past and also created deductive models based on our assumptions of human behaviour. 

Roman roads?!

During the Roman times, the northern border of the Roman empire (limes) reached within our research area. As a result, we are able to map the extent of the Roman road on our research area such that it can be used as a social predictor for archaeology. We combined the Roman road with the paleogeographic map dating to the Roman period based on the assumption that finds would most likely occur next to the road as well as the inactive river channel belts.

From the map, it was observed that many Roman finds were located close to the limes as expected. However, it was surprising that the road and many finds were located right next to the active river channel belt instead of inactive ones. This could be explained by the presence of levees (elevated lands next to river), making it reasonable for location choice of the road since it would be protected from flooding while being close to a water source. 

Next, a buffer following the Roman road passing primarily through the research area was created for four distances: 250m, 1000m, 5000m, and beyond 5000m. Using this as a reference for sites during the Roman period, we can assume that there would be a high distribution of Roman sites south of the river Rhine, distributed along the Roman road.

Through the combination of the Roman road buffer created in session 8, specifically the buffer for 250m, and the optimal river locations for settling during this time, it is possible to create a symbology which showcases where sites are most likely to be found. When compared to Roman sites, we see a large clustering around the most optimal location, which is pictured as the darkest red in the accompanying map, especially areas where the road ran alongside the river channel belt. This is also seen in the southern portion of the research area. There are also notable site clusterings north of the river, but none further than 5000m from the Roman road.

Celtic Fields

Celtic fields have been spotted in several locations from viewing the AHN3 hillshade map available from ESRI Netherlands. 

From digitising the location of these celtic fields on our research area map in QGIS, it can be observed that some Iron Age finds do correspond with the location of celtic fields. Hence, celtic fields should also be a useful social predictor for Iron Age archaeology. 

The important town of Rhenen

The vicinity of Rhenen also yields many finds dating to the Middle Ages due to the town’s historical importance. It was regarded as the most advanced stronghold for the bishop of Utrecht against the Duchy of Geldre. The commandery of the Teutonic Order (a Catholic religious institution and military society) and the Cunera church were located in Rhenen, evidencing that it was once an important town. The Cunera church was also an important pilgrimage site. 

Due to its strategic location close to the river Rhine and on the southeastern tip of the Utrechtse Heuveulrug, the town was also important in the battles between the Dutch and Germans during World War 2 (Battle of Grebbeberg, Grebbelinie) and for tobacco cultivation. As a result, the town was heavily destroyed during the war which could be assumed that most archaeological finds within the town center were also destroyed, leaving most finds to be located only around the town vicinity. 

The historical importance of Rhenen correlates with the Middle Ages as many Late Middle Ages finds from the period are found within the square where church Cunera is located, as well as near castle Tel Horst.

River courses

A simple deductive model was made for the Mesolithic period based on river courses back then. This is under the assumption that people back then would prefer to settle close to the river. It is obvious that this model does not work for the period since most finds are not located close to the active river channel (polygon in darkest red) but instead, the furthest away from the river channel.

Burial mounds

The location of bronze age burial mounds were collected from the Beschermde Gebieden - Cultuurhistorie (INSPIRE geharmoniseerd) datasetavailable via the Publieke Dienstverlening Op de Kaart (PDOK), as well as from Utrechtse Heuvelrug op de Kaart. The locations were merged in a single map before buffer zones were created based on the known burial mound locations. The buffer map works relatively well when referenced to the known Bronze Age finds from ARCHIS as indeed, a lot of finds cluster around the burial mounds. However, there is also a noticeable cluster of finds on the right (add circle) which are far away from a burial mound. This can be an indicator for more burial mounds there since the known burial mounds do align in a diagonal pattern. 

References

History of Rhenen:

https://oudrhenen.nl/historie-van-rhenen/

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhenen

Information on burial mounds:

https://www.heuvelrugopdekaart.nl

https://www.pdok.nl/introductie/-/article/beschermde-gebieden-cultuurhistorie-inspire-geharmoniseerd-

item.title: Week 4 - Landscape Characteristics
item.description:
In this week, we mapped various landscape characteristics which could have influenced site location choices by humans in the past. Soil, geomorphological, geology and paleogeographical maps were simplified to make analysis more relevant and useful for archaeology. Other landscape characteristics were also considered such as distance to water, slope and aspect. These were more challenging as they go beyond mere reclassification of existing maps, requiring us to create derived maps.

(Blog cover image credit: Samenwerkingsverband Nationale Parken, https://nationaalpark.nl/park/nationaal-park-utrechtse-heuvelrug/)

Where can we keep our feet dry?

Although we already looked at a soil map in previous sessions, the soil map of our research area is simplified further this time by categorising various parts of landscape by their degree of wetness in the past. This is based on the assumption that people would prefer to settle in areas that are dry. The column with the depth of ground water was extracted from the soil map for this.

From the reclassified map, it is easy to observe that the north-eastern part of our research area was very damp and wet which makes it unfavourable for human inhabitation. 

Good soils for habitation

From the previous complex soil map we have, we further simplified it by only including a few main soil categories. This is such that we can observe more simply where people would have preferred to settle on the landscape based on soil texture. People would not have preferred to settle on areas with clay soil since it is not suitable for agriculture. Instead, areas with sandy soils or peat are deemed more favourable. Hence, it can be observed that the northern part of our research area above the river Rhine seemed to have more favourable soil textures for habitation with mostly sand and peat compared to the south consisting mostly clay. 

If we were to add the finds and features from all periods, we can observe that the finds and features indeed reflect a relation with the soil textures and dampness of the landscape.

Living close to the river?

By comparing the paleogeographical maps with our research area, we could see that there were no changes in the river channels within our research area until time slice 5500 (3500 BCE) because the active river belt flowing from the West has not reached the research area. Before the second last Saalien glaciation, the river flow direction of the Rhine-Maas was northwest (Kasse & Griede, 2005). However, during the Saalien glaciation, an ice sheet (Fennoscadian ice sheet) reached the central part of the Netherlands and diverted the river courses of the Rhine-Maas to the West, up till today (Kasse & Griede, 2005).

item.title: Week 3 - Distortions and Manipulations
item.description:
In this week, we made important decisions in merging data from ARCHIS based on our research question as well as considering distorting factors in our maps. 

Archaeological finds or sites?

Because ARCHIS merges archaeological data from finds all together, there are several entries in the database with the same coordinates. This problem stems from having several finds locations within one archaeological site as well as having multiple finds within one find location. Creating a predictive model using that data would be problematic because sites with more finds or more intensively researched sites will outweigh other sites that might not necessarily have that many (or any) finds. Hence, we made a conscious decision to create a distribution map based on archaeological site locations rather than finds.

Afterwards, we had to create additional maps based on different categories.

Methodology

Our general methodology in separating the ARCHIS data for the predictive model is as follows:

Grouping the sites by their time periods is central for us, before we analyse the type of sites based on geology and economic activities.

We separated the data into the various ARCHIS main periods (e.g. MESO for Mesolithic, ROM for Roman period) because we believed that in each time period, there was a different type of geology that could have influenced the type of economic activities taking place then. 

Based on this, we could clearly see where in the research area did sites cluster around during a certain time period and perhaps explain this with the geology and economic activities during that time. Additionally, we could see which municipality has the most researched sites. This could be from a bias such as more development of specific towns/cities that allowed more archaeological events to take place there.

For example, we can already see how sites from the Iron Age cluster around the side of the ice push moraine as well as a small cluster around the town of Ede. This can be compared to the Roman sites which appear to have a different cluster around towards the south of our research area.

Distorting Factors

Distorting factors allow us to analyse what could have influenced the distribution pattern of sites. For this, we looked at geomorphological, soil maps and also used a mask layer on the map to check the reliability of site distribution.

Geomorphological map

From the geomorphological map, it appears that most finds are found on river banks, gullies, meltwater fans and the ice push moraine itself. Spatial distribution of finds seem to cluster near water sources while northern sand ridges do not seem to have been investigated much.

Soil maps

From the soil maps, we came to the conclusion that the Rd9 soil profile (heavy loam, light clay) yields a lot of sites which might be because of construction/development projects. Heavy clay yields the least sites since it is the least habitable soil type. We also noted down the presence of terps in our research area which indeed also showed many site occurrences.

item.title: Week 1 - Introduction to Predictive Modelling
item.description:
In archaeological contexts, predictive modeling attempts to predict the locations of archaeological sites in landscapes based on previously conducted surveys, often relying on environmental and ecological characteristics to understand the probability behind settlement placement. Predictive models are therefore useful in the context of CRM, such as in the case of the Netherlands, where the predicting concentrations of archaeological remains is important for construction and damage prevention.

Before being able to work on a predictive model, it is important to first understand how to operate the necessary software required for it, which in our case was QGIS. By manipulating and analysing various maps of the research area in QGIS, we were better able to understand the land use of the research area and how we could continue to develop a well-suited model for it.

Maps

The first basic step we had to do was to import maps. There were several types of maps we had to use such as vector, satellite imagery, elevation model (AHN), paleogeographical and geomorphological maps (And even more maps to come in weeks!) Choosing what maps to use is highly dependent on the project objective and often, multiple maps are stacked as layers to encompass a comprehensive understanding of the research area.

Understanding land use

Basic vector maps are able to show and categorise how parts of land were used.

Before and after using a clear coloured symbology to categorise land use. Choosing appropriate colours such as green for parks and blue for water sources can help direct the audience to locate significant land usage patterns. Within our research area, it is clear that there is a large forest/bos (in brown) and a Rhine river channel (middle, in blue) which can be helpful in predicting archaeology.

Additional note on metadata:

Although often we work with pre-made maps given by an organisation/online provider, it is important to assess and be critical about the quality of the data provided.

In our case, the given maps (D39G and D39E) contained relatively confusing categories of land usage. An example of this is ‘Verblijfsrecreatie’ which although translated to roughly ‘residential recreation’ in English, it can be difficult or confusing to understand the function without giving concrete examples (e.g. camping sites? Swimming pools?). It was difficult having to narrow down the 25 categories to broader 8 main categories when original given categories were not defined well. This can be resolved with addition of metadata such as a code book that provides short descriptions or examples of what the category stands for. Fortunately, this can be improved in QGIS with the ‘Value Map’ widget in Attributes Form. A drop down list of values can be created with their respective descriptions to be used in filling out attribute tables of maps.

This ensures a consistent data quality that is reproducible and minimises errors such as typos/using different words for the same category and also saves us time from typing each category individually!

Historical Maps

These maps are useful in identifying culturally significant areas in the research area such as towns and specific cultivation lands. In our research area, a few areas we identified to be interesting from the given historical map were ‘De Meent’, the ‘Tabaks Plantage’ and the ‘Buitenwaarden’ near the Rhenen municipality.

De Meent

Although the area now consists of paved roads and a residential area, it used to be a common plot of land used by farmers in Medieval times with differences in soil conditions and height.

It was interesting to discover that an attempt at mapping places of heritage, archaeology and monuments has already been done by the Gementee Utrechtse Heuvelrug! 

Tabaks Plantage

The region of Utrechtse Heuvelrug is also known to be the only region in the Netherlands where tobacco was planted, and this is reflected in the historical map showing the tobacco plantation. Although the land is now currently part of a forest.

Buitenwaarden

Originally a floodplain of the adjacent river Rhine channel, it is now a nature reserve. It is also part of the transition between the river and forest landscape.

There are a lot more areas in the map waiting to be explored, which can tell us a lot about the context of current and historical land use.

item.title: Week 2 - The Wonders of ARCHIS!
item.description:
During this week, we got to look into the ARCHIS (Het Archeologisch Informatiesysteem) database which basically contains all information of archaeological activity that takes place in the Netherlands.

We downloaded and looked at information from version 3 of ARCHIS, which is the latest version. Before we bore you with additional details, here is a visual condensed overview of what we got out of the data:

The Late Middle Ages recorded to be the largest percentage of sites followed by the Iron Age. Paleolithic and Mesolithic sites are the most rarely recorded. Again, these are the known recorded sites and do not necessarily represent the true archaeological record of the area. This might be due to bias and other factors like site preservation.

It is interesting to also note that Rhenen has almost half of the recorded sites from the municipalities within our research area while Veenendaal is the least (which was not surprising during our research because we could barely find anything documented there). More research is needed to analyse why exactly are the results so, if they stem from bias or other factors.

Moving on to looking at several reports and archaeological activities within the research area, we recorded some notable finds and sites from each municipality by looking through the ARCHIS database as well as other maps documenting monuments and archaeology (e.g. Rijksmonument, Utrechtse Heuvelrug op de Kaart etc.)

Utrechtse-Heuvelrug

We read about Leersum and Amerongen in this region. Leersum notably has been habitated since the Bronze Age to the Merovingian period.

Buren

Buren mostly consisted of Roman and Middle Ages finds, with a specific Roman coin hoard found recently in 2017.

Veenendaal

Pottery fragments and crockery were found near Fort aan de Buurtsteeg dating to 18-19th centuries. Expectation for Nieuwe Tijd finds are high.

Ede

Very little Iron Age research has been done here despite an Iron Age found here with two huts dated to the end of the 5th century CE.

Rhenen

An Iron Age settlement was found here in 2018 although the main building of the settlement was not found. Hence, they expect the main building to be found someday in the vicinity of the site.

Tiel

A Batavian burial ground site was located here. Gully deposits from 1250-800 BCE also found here. Finds from Roman period and Late Middle Ages-Nieuwe Tijd.

Protected Monuments

Also during this session, legally protected monuments were mapped in the research area using the WFS client of the RCE in QGIS. Monuments outside of the bounds of the research area were removed through clipping; the 11 monuments within were then described with the attributes dating and type, based on their descriptions in a monument registry. A categorized symbology was made using this information, which helped to visualize the dates and type of sites in this region. This was notably difficult because there were instances of multiple phases of occupation and multiple finds from one site, which was hard to simplify into a “main date” or “main type” for a visual analysis.

item.title: Geology of the Netherlands
item.description:
Do you struggle in understanding how the landscape of the Netherlands came to be about today? Don’t worry, you’re not alone.

Having to summarise and explain about the geology of the Netherlands in general over the span of thousands of years seem to be a daunting task, but it is easy to just think about the (somewhat recent) general geology of the Netherlands in two phases (there are other events that caused many other things to happen but we are not geologists and will not attempt to explain those):

Pleistocene

Two glacials (ice age, very cold periods) happened during this time, namely the Saalien and Weichselian. The Weichselian came first but didn’t result in ice reaching the Netherlands. The Netherlands was just a very cold and dry desert with strong winds transporting cover sand (aeolian deposits) especially towards the south (present day Limburg) which also gave rise to the highly fertile loess (silt) there. 

During the Saalien glacial, the ice did reach the Netherlands and the glaciers pushed up and transported sediment which created ridges known as ice-push moraines such as the one found in Utrechtse Heuvelrug that is within our research area! 

Holocene

Temperatures rose during the Holocene which resulted in the retreat of the glaciers from the ice age and rising sea levels. The Netherlands was flooded as a result which allowed peat formation and deposition of sediment through water (fluvial and marine deposits)

How is geology relevant in our archaeological research?

The red areas have Pleistocene deposits on the surface which are well-covered by sediment (either by wind/water/peat etc.) and hence, archaeology is deemed to be better preserved in these areas. The northern part of our research area interestingly falls under the red region as well.

Our research area also then proves to be an interesting case study because it consists of most of the geological features of the Netherlands to be studied. From a moraine plateau, flood plains, river basins, cover sand as well as peat. Understanding landscape features and the processes which they are formed allows us to better associate and predict archaeology with them.

item.title: About
item.description:
Who are we? What do we do?

Grutto Archeologie is a (fictional) archaeological prospection company run by NyAnna Beeman and Shelene Low. Inspired by the Grutto (Black-tailed godwit), the threatened national bird of the Netherlands, we aim to use predictive modelling as a method to help with preserving archaeology in the Netherlands which can be threatened by various development and construction projects.

Technical stuff

This blog is made possible with RStudio and the Blogdown R package. The blog makes use of a free Hugo theme from Jimmy Cai. Updates of the blog are continuously deployed through GitHub and the source code is publicly available.
